title: The Sun's Influence: Seasons and Breezes
competency: Explain how the tilt of the Earth relative to its orbit affects the intensity of sunlight and the length of daytime; and how solar energy contributes to the occurrence of land and sea breezes, monsoons, and the ITCZ.
objectives: Explain how the 23.5-degree tilt of the Earth causes seasons.
Describe the relationship between the angle of the sun's rays and the intensity of heat received.
Differentiate between land breeze and sea breeze.
Identify the characteristics of the Amihan and Habagat monsoons.
Explain the importance of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) to the Philippines.
introduction: The Sun is the engine that drives Earth's climate and weather. Because the Earth is tilted and revolves around the Sun, different parts of the world receive different amounts of energy at different times of the year. This energy also causes the movement of air, creating breezes and seasonal wind patterns known as monsoons.
content:
1. Why do we have Seasons?

Seasons are caused by the 23.5-degree tilt of the Earth’s axis as it revolves around the Sun. It is NOT caused by the distance of the Earth from the Sun.

  • Direct Rays: When a hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, it receives vertical or direct rays. This results in higher solar intensity, longer daytime, and warmer temperatures (Summer).
  • Slanted Rays: When a hemisphere is tilted away, it receives slanted rays. The energy is spread over a larger area, resulting in shorter days and cooler temperatures (Winter).

2. Land and Sea Breezes

These are local winds caused by the differential heating of land and water:

  • Sea Breeze (Daytime): Land heats up faster than water. Warm air over land rises (Low Pressure), and cool air from the sea moves in to replace it.
  • Land Breeze (Nighttime): Land cools down faster than water. Warm air over the sea rises, and cool air from the land moves out toward the sea.

3. Monsoons in the Philippines

Monsoons are seasonal wind patterns that affect large regions:

  • Amihan (Northeast Monsoon): Occurs from October to March. It brings cool, dry air from Siberia and China toward the Philippines.
  • Habagat (Southwest Monsoon): Occurs from June to September. It brings warm, moist air from the Indian Ocean, resulting in heavy rains.

4. The ITCZ

The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is a belt of low pressure near the equator where the trade winds from the Northern and Southern Hemispheres meet. It is characterized by frequent thunderstorms and heavy rainfall.

examples.title: Summer Solstice
examples.description: Around June 21, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted at its maximum toward the Sun, resulting in the longest day of the year in the Philippines.

examples.title: The Habagat Effect
examples.description: During the months of July and August, the Southwest Monsoon often causes class cancellations in the Philippines due to continuous heavy rainfall and flooding.

keyTerms.definition: The imaginary line through the center of the Earth around which it rotates.
The movement of the Earth around the Sun, taking approximately 365.25 days.
The transfer of heat by the movement of air or water currents.

keyConcepts: The tilt of the Earth causes the change in the length of daytime and the intensity of sunlight.
Air always moves from an area of High Pressure (cool air) to an area of Low Pressure (warm air).
The movement of the ITCZ follows the location of the most intense sunlight on Earth.
summary: The Earth's tilt and revolution create the seasons by changing how sunlight hits the surface. On a smaller scale, the uneven heating of land and water creates breezes and monsoons. In the tropics, the ITCZ serves as a major weather system bringing rain and thunderstorms.
